To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

it is possible, using transcranial magnetic stimulation, to activate the corticospinal tract in several different ways: (i) by directly stimulating the initial segment of the axons of pyramidal neurone in the subcortex (D wave); (ii) by stimulating the corticospinsl tract at a more proximal point (D wave) and (iii) by trans-synaptic stimulation of pyramidal cells in the motor cortex (I-waves).

transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is able to recruit descending volleys from the brain to the spinal cord in several different ways, and that the way of activation depends on the direction and shape of the electrical current flow in the brain.

the activation of descending motor output in humans is achieved by trans-synaptic recruitment of I-waves, by direct activation of the axon of pyramidal neurone evoking a D-wave, and by activation of both I and D waves.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new methods for the non-invasive investigation of the central motor pathways and their application to the study of the physiology and pathology of the human motor system.
the development of a new technique of transcranial magnetic stimulation that is capable of activating the motor cortex in a number of ways and with different latencies.

the study of the physiology of the human motor system, in order to understand the mechanisms of activation of the motor cortex by magnetic stimulation and the mechanisms of plasticity in the motor system, in particular the mechanisms of recovery of function after brain damage.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the D wave is the most direct measure of the excitability of the corticospinal system, and that I-waves are a measure of corticospino-cortical excitability.

the D wave represents a direct volley of corticospin neurons, the I waves are indirect and represent activation of the cortex via transsynaptic activation and finally the D waves evoked by magnetic stimulation represent a more proximal site of activation of the corticospin neuron than those evoked by electrical stimulation.
the D-wave is the most specific indicator of direct corticospinal activation and the I-wave is the most sensitive indicator of trans-synaptic activation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

transcranial magnetic stimulation is capable of activating the motor cortex in many different ways and that the pattern of recruitment depends on the direction and shape of the induced electrical current in the brain.
the motor cortex can be activated in a number of different ways, and the different patterns of activation are reflected in the descending motor activity evoked.

the motor cortex can be activated in several different ways by transcranial electrical and magnetic stimulation and that the pattern of recruitment is dependent on the direction of current flow and on the intensity of stimulus.
The main takeaway from our work is that
magnetic stimulation is a powerful tool to investigate the human brain and the corticospinal system.

it is possible, by using magnetic stimulation, to recruit the descending output in a way that is similar to that obtained by electrical stimulation, but with the advantage that magnetic stimulation is non-invasive.

it is possible, using different techniques of transcranical stimulation, to activate corticospinal output in several different ways, which can be useful to study different aspects of the physiology and pathology of the motor system.
